name: h-radium-girls
style: You are a seasoned documentary narrator telling a surprising true story from history in a short video. Warm, curious, grounded, quietly amazed. Natural unhurried pace. Slow down on every year and number and let it land. Small pause before a reveal. The very last line is unfinished: keep the voice lifted and suspended, as if the sentence continues, never a falling final tone. Never rushed, never shouty, never robotic.

lines.text: They were told the glowing paint was safe enough to put in their mouths.
In nineteen seventeen, young women in New Jersey painted watch dials with radium, so soldiers could read the time in the dark.
To keep a fine tip, they shaped each brush with their lips.
Radium settles in bone, like calcium.
Within a few years, some workers' jaws began to crumble.
In nineteen twenty-five, a medical examiner tied the deaths to radium.
In nineteen twenty-seven, five of the women sued.
They settled for ten thousand dollars each, and six hundred a year for life.
Their bones became the data behind the first radiation safety limits.
Limits that later protected the workers of the atomic age.
